sections.h: Sirach: the father who keeps the whip on his son
sections.b: Ben Sira's teaching on sons (Sirach 30:1–13) is the sternest in the wisdom books. A father who loves his son "will keep the whip on him," should "bruise his ribs while he is still small," and must not laugh along with him or give him free rein. The reward is a son "like himself" who carries on his name after death (30:4–6). The teaching takes up Proverbs 13:24 and 23:13–14 and goes further in detail. The New Testament keeps discipline as love (Hebrews 12:5–11) but adds a check on fathers (Ephesians 6:4). Ben Sira wrote for wealthy Jerusalem households about 190 BC, where an unruly heir could ruin a family.

Sirach 30:33–40 (KJV 33:24–31) gives a slave owner's advice: "bread, discipline and work" for a slave, the yoke and the rack for a bad one, heavier shackles for the disobedient. Then the tone turns: "do not go too far with anyone," and "If you have a slave, treat him like yourself," for you need him "as you need your own life"; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read "like a brother." The harsh rules go beyond the Law's limits on masters (Exodus 21:20, 26–27); the closing lines lean toward Job 31:13–15 and Paul's letter to Philemon.
sections.refs: Sirach 30:33–40; Exodus 21:20–27; Deuteronomy 15:12–15; Job 31:13–15; Philemon 1:16; Colossians 4:1

sections.b: Ben Sira warns that dreams "give fools wings": to trust them is to grab at a shadow or chase the wind, for a dream is only "the likeness of a face before a face" (Sirach 31:1–3). He puts dreams with divination and omens (31:5; compare Deuteronomy 18:10) but leaves room for a dream "sent from the Most High" (31:6), as the Bible's dreams of Joseph and Daniel were. The sure guide is the law (31:8; compare Deuteronomy 13:1–5 and Jeremiah 23:28).
sections.refs: Sirach 31:1–8; Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Deuteronomy 18:10; Jeremiah 23:25–28; Ecclesiastes 5:7; Numbers 12:6

sections.h: Sirach: the bread of the poor
sections.b: Sirach 31:21–27 (KJV 34:18–22) is among the sharpest words on justice outside the Hebrew Bible. A sacrifice from ill-gotten goods is "an offering made in mockery"; offering what belongs to the poor is like "Killing a son in front of his father"; the bread of the needy is the poor man's life, and whoever takes it, or holds back a hired man's pay, "sheds blood." In 1514 Bartolomé de las Casas, studying this passage for a Pentecost sermon, gave up his slaves and his grant of native labor in Spain's American colonies.

sections.h: Sirach: the offering of keeping the law
sections.b: Ben Sira loved the temple and its worship (Sirach 50:1–21), yet he insists that God refuses offerings from injustice (31:21–24) and that "a great number of sacrifices does not make atonement for sins" (31:23). Keeping the law is itself many offerings, repaying a kindness is a grain offering, alms are "a sacrifice of praise," and turning from wrong "makes atonement" (32:1–5). But the commanded offerings must still be brought: "Do not appear before the Lord with empty hands" (32:6), with a glad face and a good eye (32:10–12). Hebrews 13:15–16 joins praise and sharing as sacrifices in the same way.
sections.refs: Sirach 31:21–24; Sirach 32:1–13; 1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6; Hebrews 13:15–16; Deuteronomy 16:16–17

sections.b: Sirach 32:14–26 (KJV 35:12–20) pictures God as the judge who cannot be bribed. He "will never ignore the cry of an orphan, / nor a widow as she pours out her words"; her tears run down her cheek and her outcry rises against the one who caused them. The prayer of the humble goes through the clouds and does not rest until God acts; "the Lord will not delay, / nor will he be patient with them." Luke's parable of the widow and the crooked judge (Luke 18:1–8) uses the same picture and the same Greek phrase.

sections.h: Sirach: the prayer that goes through the clouds
sections.b: "The prayer of the humble has gone through the clouds" (Sirach 32:21) is Ben Sira's best-known line on prayer: it will not be comforted until it comes near, or leave until the Most High looks into it. The same chapters hold a long prayer for Israel, split in the Greek order into Sirach 33:1–13 and 36:16–22: have mercy, show your power to the nations, gather the tribes of Jacob, fill Zion with your glory, "so that everyone on earth will know / that you are the Lord, God of all the ages."

Ben Sira's teaching on wine (Sirach 34:25–31; KJV 31:25–31) is balanced. "Wine is as good as life to people / if you drink it in its proper measure"; "It was created for human gladness" (34:27), as Psalm 104:15 says. But "Do not play the hero over wine, / for wine has brought down many" (34:25); too much brings a bitter soul, rage and wounds (34:29–30). At a wine party, do not scold or shame your neighbor (34:31). The banquet chapter that follows praises music over wine like a jewel set in gold (35:5–6).
sections.refs: Sirach 34:25–31; Sirach 35:5–6; Psalm 104:15; Judges 9:13; Proverbs 23:29–35; Isaiah 5:22

sections.h: Sirach: manners at a great table
sections.b: Sirach 34:12–24 and 35:1–13 (KJV 31:12–32:13) are a guide to the banquets of Jerusalem's upper class. Do not gobble, grab or "jostle him in the bowl" (34:14, the word of Mark 14:20); "Know what your neighbor wants by what you want yourself" (34:15; the Hebrew has "know your neighbor as yourself"); stop first, eat little and sleep well. If made leader of the feast, serve the guests before you sit (35:1–2; compare John 2:8–9 and Luke 22:26). Let the old speak with knowledge and the young barely at all, and at the end bless the Maker who fills you with good things (35:13).
sections.refs: Sirach 34:12–24; Sirach 35:1–13; Proverbs 23:1–3; Mark 14:20; Luke 14:7–11; John 2:8–10; Deuteronomy 8:10

sections.b: Ben Sira (Sirach 34:1–11; KJV 31:1–11) pictures the rich man awake at night over his money, and warns that "Whoever loves gold will not be found in the right." Gold is "a log that trips up those who sacrifice to it" (34:7). Yet he praises the rare rich man "found with no blemish, / who did not run after gold" (34:8): "Who is he? Let us call him blessed!" Where the Greek has "gold," the Hebrew of 34:8 has mamon, the word behind Jesus' saying about God and wealth (Matthew 6:24).
sections.refs: Sirach 34:1–11; Matthew 6:24; Luke 16:13; Mark 10:23–27; 1 Timothy 6:9–10; Luke 12:16–21

sections.h: Sirach: the law like the Urim
sections.b: In Sirach 36:3 (KJV 33:3) the wise man's trust in the law is compared to an oracle. Vaticanus reads "as an inquiry made by the righteous," but Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read the Septuagint's word for the Urim (as in Numbers 27:21), and the Hebrew of the Cairo Genizah says plainly, "his law is like the Urim in the breastpiece." For Ben Sira, in an age with no Urim to consult (Ezra 2:63), the law gives the sure answers that the high priest's lots once gave.

sections.h: Sirach: 'Gather all the tribes of Jacob'
sections.b: Ben Sira's prayer for Israel asks, "Gather all the tribes of Jacob" (Sirach 33:13), and, after the break caused by the Greek order, "you will give them their inheritance as at the beginning" (36:16; KJV 36:11). Centuries after the northern tribes were scattered, a Jerusalem scribe still prayed for all twelve. He gives Elijah the task of restoring them (48:10). The hope stands behind Matthew 19:28 and John 11:52.
sections.refs: Sirach 33:13; Sirach 36:16; Sirach 48:10; Isaiah 11:12; Isaiah 49:6; Matthew 19:28; John 11:52

sections.h: Sirach: clay in the potter's hand
sections.b: Sirach 36:7–15 (KJV 33:7–15) explains why one day is holy and another ordinary, though all get their light from the sun: the Lord set them apart. So with people: all are from the soil, but "Some he blessed and lifted up; / some he set apart as holy and drew near to himself. / Some he cursed and humbled." "As clay is in the potter's hand," so are human beings in their Maker's hand (36:13), the image of Jeremiah 18:6 and Romans 9:21. Ben Sira had also taught that God left humanity in the hand of its own choice (Sirach 15:14), and he does not explain how the two fit.
sections.refs: Sirach 36:7–15; Sirach 15:14; Jeremiah 18:1–10; Isaiah 45:9; Wisdom of Solomon 15:7; Romans 9:20–21

sections.h: Sirach: a helper who is his match
sections.b: Sirach 36:26–31 (KJV 36:21–26) praises a good wife in the words of Genesis 2:18: the man who gets a wife has "a helper who is his match and a pillar to lean on" (36:29, the exact Greek of the Septuagint). If kindness is on her tongue, her husband is luckier than other men (36:28; compare Proverbs 31:26). Without a wife, "a man wanders about groaning" (36:30); the Hebrew uses the words God spoke to Cain, na' wanad, a wanderer and a drifter (Genesis 4:12). The passage assumes arranged marriage: "A woman will accept any male, / but one daughter is better than another" (36:26).
sections.refs: Sirach 36:26–31; Genesis 2:18; Genesis 4:12; Proverbs 18:22; Proverbs 19:14; Proverbs 31:26

sections.b: In Sirach 30–36 the Greek manuscripts have two long blocks in the reverse order from the Hebrew and the Latin, which the KJV and most English Bibles follow. After Sirach 30:24, the Greek goes on with the block the KJV prints as 33:16–36:11 (on this site 30:25–33:13), and only then gives KJV 30:25–33:15 (here 34:1–36:15). Verse 36:16 joins the two: its first half belongs before 30:25 and its second half after 33:13. Rahlfs, the Göttingen edition and Orthodox Bibles keep the Greek numbers; this site does too, and gives the KJV numbers in a note at the start of each displaced block.

sections.h: Sirach: alms as a sacrifice of praise
sections.b: "Whoever gives alms offers a sacrifice of praise" (Sirach 32:4): alms stand beside the temple offerings as a gift God accepts, as Tobit 4:11 and Hebrews 13:16 also say. The honest rich man's alms will be told by the assembly (34:11), a public honor that Jesus' "keep your left hand from knowing" (Matthew 6:3) treats more warily. For the question whether alms take away sin (Sirach 3:30), see the card in Tobit 4.
sections.refs: Sirach 32:4; Sirach 34:11; Sirach 3:30; Tobit 4:10–11; Hebrews 13:16; Matthew 6:1–4

sections.b: Before his chapter on the physician (Sirach 38:1–15), Ben Sira praises health: "Better a poor man, healthy and strong of build, / than a rich man scourged in his own body"; "No riches beat a body in good health" (30:14–16). A glad heart is a person's life, and grief and worry age the body (30:21–24; compare Proverbs 17:22). Moderate eating gives healthy sleep, while the greedy man suffers sleeplessness, nausea (cholera) and cramps (34:19–21).

Ben Sira rarely speaks of himself, but two passages in these chapters do. He calls himself the last of Israel's teachers, a gleaner behind the grape pickers who by the Lord's blessing still filled the winepress, and says his toil was "for everyone who is looking for instruction" (Sirach 30:25–26, with 36:16; KJV 33:16–17). He has traveled: "I have seen much in my wanderings, / and my understanding goes beyond my words," and he often came near to death (31:12–13; KJV 34:11–12). He addresses "the great men of the people" and "the leaders of the assembly" (30:27), the Jerusalem elite whose sons he taught.
